title: Spot wrong-length codes with LEN
summary: Count the characters in SKU codes with LEN and flag any code that is the wrong length with IF.

blocks.text: The Nairobi warehouse has sent a stock file with SKU codes for the new season. Our SKU standard is nine characters, for example SN-450-42: two letters, a hyphen, three digits, a hyphen and a two-digit size.

A code with a missing or extra character will not match anything in the price list or the stock system. Before the file is loaded, you need a quick way to find the odd ones out. LEN counts characters, and IF turns the count into a clear flag.

items: Objective: measure text with LEN and flag wrong-length codes with IF.
You pass the mission at 75% or more in the Assessment.

blocks.text: LEN returns the number of characters in the text. Letters, digits, hyphens and spaces all count as one character each.

blocks.caption: What LEN returns for some codes

blocks.text: Count the characters in A2. If the count equals 9 show OK, otherwise show Check. In your sheet the 9 sits in a cell (F1) so you can change the standard without editing every formula.

items: Spaces count. A code typed as "SL 075 42" has two spaces inside it, so LEN counts 9 even though it does not look like a hyphen code. You will meet spaces again in the TRIM mission.
LEN also works on numbers: it counts the characters as shown, so LEN(1050) is 4.
Tip: a code like 00123 typed as a number loses its leading zeros and becomes 123, so LEN gives 3. To keep leading zeros, type the code as text, for example with a leading apostrophe: '00123.
A length check only tells you something is wrong. It does not say what. Use it to find rows to inspect.

blocks.text: Type numbers without commas or spaces, for example 12.

items: LEN(text) counts characters, including hyphens and spaces.
IF(LEN(A2)=n, "OK", "Check") flags codes that are not exactly n characters long.
Keep the standard length in an input cell and fix it with $ signs.
LEN counts numbers as shown; leading zeros are lost unless the value is typed as text.

blocks.text: A length check is the cheapest data-quality test you can run: it catches typos before they reach the price list.

items.prompt: Cell A2 holds SN-45-42. What does =IF(LEN(A2)=9,"OK","Check") show?
Why does the check formula point at $F$1 instead of typing 9 inside it?

options.label: So the standard length can be changed in one cell and every check updates
Because LEN will not work without a cell reference
Because it makes LEN count faster
Because it turns the length into text
